name: Mexoryl SX (ecamsule)
lead: Ecamsule, known commercially as Mexoryl SX (INCI name terephthalylidene dicamphor sulfonic acid), is a water-soluble UVA filter developed by L'Oreal. Grokipedia states it absorbs with a peak near 345 nm and was developed and patented in 1982.[1]

It has been studied more extensively than many newer filters. A 1998 study reported protection of human skin against repeated sub-erythemal UVA doses, a 2008 review summarised clinical results of Mexoryl SX sunscreens, and a 2019 JAMA trial found that ecamsule and three other sunscreen ingredients reached plasma concentrations above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold under maximal-use conditions.[2][3][4]
infobox: Approved via L'Oreal drug applications per cited source[1]

paras: Ecamsule is a camphor-derived molecule with sulfonic acid groups, usually neutralised so it dissolves in the water phase of formulations.[1] It is commonly paired with other filters, including Mexoryl XL.[1]

Grokipedia reports that L'Oreal developed and patented ecamsule in 1982 and that the US FDA approved it in 2006 through new drug applications for specific L'Oreal products.[1] Because that source is AI-generated, dates should be treated as provisional.

In a 1998 study, volunteers received repeated sub-erythemal UVA exposures over 13 weeks and the authors evaluated whether Mexoryl SX protected against resulting skin changes.[2] A 2008 review summarised clinical studies of Mexoryl SX sunscreens against UV-induced skin effects.[4] A 2000 study of a full-spectrum daily cream reported protection against biological changes involved in photoaging.[5] A 2004 paper examined prevention of UV-induced pigmentation.[6] A photoprovocation study evaluated sunscreens in patients with photosensitive lupus erythematosus.[7]

A 2003 study compared percutaneous absorption in human volunteers with in vitro data.[8] The 2019 JAMA randomised trial measured blood levels of avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene and ecamsule from four sunscreens; the paper discusses the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold for further toxicology work.[3] A 2010 photopatch study included Anthelios SX, which contains Mexoryl SX, and reported true photoallergy to sunscreens as rare.[9]

Human studies include a 1998 repeated-UVA exposure study, a 2000 photoaging-cream study, a 2000 lupus photoprovocation study, a 2004 pigmentation study, a 2003 absorption study, the 2019 JAMA absorption trial and a 2008 review.[2][3][4][5][6][7][8]

quick.overview:
Mexoryl SX is a UVA filter developed by L'Oreal and used in products such as Anthelios and La Roche-Posay sunscreens. It is one of the few newer UVA filters available in the US.

It has more human data than most newer filters, including studies on UVA-induced skin changes, pigmentation and photoaging markers.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UVA (peak near 345 nm) and is described as photostable; it dissolves in the water phase of formulations.
quick.risks: A 2019 JAMA trial found it was detectable in blood after maximal-use application, above the FDA threshold for further testing; the paper does not conclude this indicates harm. Photoallergy to sunscreens is described as rare.
